text:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Mama set down a bowl of red strawberries. Aubrey smelled them with her nose. "Yummy smell," she said. She heard them plop in the bowl with her ears. She touched one with her fingers. It felt bumpy and cool.

But Aubrey had a problem. She did not want the green tops cut off. "Try one first," said Mama. "Pass me the big one," Aubrey said. Mama passed it over. Aubrey held her nose closed with her fingers. She took a bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. "Oh!" she said. She let go of her nose. She took another bite. Now it tasted sweet and strong. "It's back!" she said. She took a big bite and smiled. "Lucky me, strawberries taste so good."

Henry went to the library today. Yesterday he could not go, because it rained. Today the sun was out, and Mom held his hand.

"Good morning," said the man at the desk. Henry looked around. It was morning, and he had eaten breakfast at home. He had eaten eggs, and he had licked his spoon clean.

Henry wanted the bear book. Last week the bear book was gone. Now the shelf was empty again.

"Where is the bear book?" Henry asked.

"It comes back tomorrow," said the man. "Someone is reading it now."

"Tomorrow is a whole sleep away," said Mom with a smile.

Henry found a duck book instead. He sat on the soft rug. He turned the pages slowly. The duck said quack, and Henry laughed.

"Now we read," said Mom. "Later we can take the duck book home."

"Tomorrow we come back for bears?" Henry asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow."

Henry patted the cover. "See you tomorrow, bear book," he whispered.

Sara had a garden at the farm. She dug little holes in the brown soil. She put tomato seeds in one hole. She put carrot seeds in another hole. Then she watered them with a small can.

The next day, Sara forgot her spots. "Where did my tomatoes go?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. He helped her make picture labels. Each label had a tomato or a carrot on it. "A label stuck in the soil shows what was planted in each spot," said Grandpa. Sara pushed a tomato label into the dirt. Then she pushed a carrot label in too. "Now I know, now I know!" she sang.

Little green sprouts came up. Sara looked at the labels. The tomato sprout grew by the tomato label. The carrot sprout grew by the carrot label. "Hello, little tomato," she said. A pretty butterfly landed on the tomato leaf. It stayed there for a long time. Sara watered her sprouts and whispered, "Grow big, grow big."

Georgia sat on Grandma's big striped chair. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Uncle Sam clapped. Grandma clapped. Georgia clapped too.

Georgia wanted to know who would win. She asked, "Who won the game?" Uncle Sam said, "Not yet. We have to wait." So Georgia waited. She hugged her soft bear. She watched the TV.

The game went on and on. It was night outside now. Daddy pointed at the screen. "Look. Both teams have the same score," he said. Georgia looked. The numbers were the same. Same and same.

"Who won now?" Georgia asked. Grandma smiled and said, "Nobody won. When both teams have the same score, it is called a tie." Georgia said the word slowly. "A tie." She liked that word.

Then one team kicked the ball, and it went in! The big number changed. Everyone jumped up. Uncle Sam lifted his arms. Grandma laughed out loud. Georgia stood on the chair cushion, and Grandma said, "Feet on the floor, sweetheart." So Georgia slid down and stood by Grandma's knee.

"It is not a tie now!" Georgia said. "That team has more!" Everyone clapped for her. Georgia clapped too, and hugged her bear tight.

Stella stood by the play table. Three kids were there. They rocked a baby doll and stirred a pot.

Stella wanted to play too. She walked closer. She stood very still. Nobody looked up.

She touched the doll's blanket. The kids kept stirring. Stella felt like crying a tiny bit.

Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend I am the doctor," she said.

Ben looked up fast. "Okay! The baby has a scratch on her knee."

Stella got a bandage from the toy box. She patted the doll. "All better now."

"You are a lucky baby," said Mia. "The doctor came today."

Then Mia held up a spoon. "Let's pretend this soup is magic soup!"

The pot bubbled with giggles. Stella stirred and stirred. The kitchen got very busy.

"More soup, Doctor?" Ben asked.

"Yes please," said Stella. "Magic soup for everyone."

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She wanted to find a book all by herself. The bookshop was warm and friendly. Books sat on the shelves like little rows of colors.

Brooklyn found a big book of letters. She pointed at the first one. "That is A," she said. "A goes a, a, apple." Dad smiled. She turned the pages. B went buh. C went kuh. She sang the letter song all the way to P. Then she stopped. "The end," she said. She shut the book.

Dad shook his head. "Not yet," he said. "Keep going." Brooklyn opened the book again. She sang past P. Q went kwuh. R went ruh. Her voice got louder. She kept turning pages. S, T, U, all the way on.

Then she saw the last page. "Z!" she shouted. "The song ends at Z!" A lady at the desk looked up and clapped. Brooklyn laughed. The alphabet started with A and ended with Z. Who knew there were so many letters hiding after P?

At dinner, Brooklyn spelled her name with peas on her plate. "B, R, O," she said. Dad added the rest. Brooklyn ate the letter O first.

Andrew went to the little pool by the lake. His dad came too. Andrew wanted to get in the water all by himself.

First Andrew sat on the edge. He pushed and pushed. His arms were too small. He could not climb out over the side. A duck went pop into the lake, but Andrew stayed stuck.

Then Andrew saw the ladder. It went right into the water. He put his foot on the first step. Then the next step. Step by step, he climbed down into the pool. "I did it!" said Andrew. He held the rail and kicked his feet. He was not shy anymore.

When it was time to go, Andrew used the steps. Up, up, up he went. It was easy. "The steps help you get in and out of the water," said Dad. Andrew yawned a big yawn. He was ready for his nap. He waved to the duck and said, "Bye bye, lake."

Iris did not want to sleep. She pulled on her shoe under the blanket. "Is today library day?" she asked.

Mom sat on the bed. "Yes, it is today," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now."

Iris looked out the window. The sky was dark. "But now is night," she said.

"The library was this morning," said Mom. "We read the bear book. That was today, too."

Iris thought hard. This morning was today. Now was today too. One day could hold both! She wiggled her toes. "Yesterday we went to the park," she said. "My hands got sticky from the pear."

"That's right," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done."

"Tomorrow I want new books," said Iris.

"Tomorrow comes later," said Mom. "Sleep now, and tomorrow will come."

Iris pulled off her shoe and set it by the bed. She closed her eyes. Mom tickled her nose with a soft kiss.

"Later, I will dream about books," said Iris.

"Yes," said Mom. "Later is a good time for dreams."

Iris hugged her bear and waited. She heard the house go quiet. One tick at a time, the clock walked toward tomorrow.

"Goodnight, today," Iris whispered.

Romy wanted her teddy bear. Teddy was stuck on the big shelf. The shelf was up high. Romy was small.

Romy tried to jump. She went up a tiny bit. Then she came right back down. "Up and down are opposites," said her brother, Tom. "Watch me." Tom climbed up the ladder. He reached teddy. Then he slid down the slide. Fast!

Romy looked at the toy train. She pushed it slow. Then she pushed it fast. It went under the little chair. Romy laughed.

Then the door opened. Dad came in with cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," said Dad. He held the cup. Romy touched the cold window first. Then she sipped. "Warm now," she said.

But there was a surprise in her cup. A tiny marshmallow was hiding at the bottom. "One more?" asked Dad. Romy held out her cup and smiled.

Willow's teacher put out a big red box. "Let's sort our toys," said Miss Pim. Willow peeked inside. She saw cars, trucks and one yellow banana. The banana was a pretend banana, but it was not a toy car.

Willow picked up a car. It had round wheels. She picked up the truck. It had round wheels too. Then she held up the banana. "You are the odd one out," she said. "You do not belong with the cars." Miss Pim smiled. "Yes, Willow. The odd one out is the thing that does not belong in a group."

Next, Willow looked at the animal shelf. She saw a cat, a dog and a rubber duck. All the animals were soft. The duck was not. "Hello, odd one out," said Willow. She moved the duck to the toy box. It sat there with a ball and a drum. Now every group had things that were the same.

At snack time, Willow looked at her plate. There were apples, grapes and a little toy spoon. "Miss Pim," she called softly, "I found one more." The teacher laughed. "Put it back in the toy bin." Willow carried the spoon over and dropped it in. "There," she said. "Now all my foods are just foods."

Layla stood in the kitchen. She wanted to know what Mom was making. She used her eyes to look. She saw a big pot on the stove. Mom stirred it. It was too heavy for Layla to lift.

Layla used her ears to listen. She heard the pot go pop, pop, pop. She used her nose to smell. Mmm, it smelled like soup.

"Smell with your nostrils," said Mom. "Your nose has two openings called nostrils."

Layla touched her nose. She felt two little holes. She wanted to count them. Mom held up a small mirror. Layla looked in. She saw one opening. She saw two. Two nostrils!

Then Mom gave her a taste. Layla used her tongue. It was warm soup.

"Yum!" said Layla. She jumped up and down. "Is this a gift?"

"Yes," said Mom. "A gift from our kitchen."

Charlie ran to soccer practice. Coach Nina had a big red ball. "One ball, one game," she said. "Everyone gets a turn to kick it."

Charlie wanted to kick first. He ran up fast. He grabbed at the ball with both hands. "Not yet," said Coach Nina. "Maya is first today."

Charlie sat down on the grass. Waiting felt so long. He puffed out his cheeks like a frog.

Then he saw some cones nearby. He lined them up. He put a pinecone on top of each one. "Look, a tower with a star shape on this one," he said. Maya laughed and kicked the ball far. Then Ben kicked it. Then it was almost his turn, and his tower was done.

"Charlie, your turn," said Coach Nina. Charlie jumped up. He ran to the ball. He sent it rolling all the way to Maya. She sent it back.

"Nice kick," said Maya. "Nice tower," said Charlie. "You are a friendly kick sender."

After practice, Charlie waved goodbye. "Same time next week," said Coach Nina. "And I get to build the tower," said Maya.

Brooklyn waited at the bus stop with her grandma. It was cold. "Time for your coat," said Grandma. Brooklyn picked it up. One arm in. One arm in. Now the zipper. She pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. She tried again. Slowly it went zip, zip, zip, all the way to the top. "I did it," said Brooklyn.

Then she got warm and took the coat off. She dropped it on the ground. A furry dog walked by. A boy dropped his carrot. People's feet went tap, tap, tap. Brooklyn's coat went under the bench. Soon she could not see it. "Where is my coat?" she asked. She looked down. She looked under. There it was, dusty on the ground.

The bus came near. Brooklyn put her coat on again. One arm in. One arm in. Zip, zip, zip. Then she saw a little hook on the bus stop pole. She hung her coat on the hook. It stayed up high. It did not touch the ground. "My coat is safe," she said. Grandma smiled. "Bus is here," she said. "I dream of warm cocoa at home," said Brooklyn. She took her coat off the hook and climbed the bus steps.

Parker stood by the little green pool in his backyard. His big sister was having a swim party, and a lifeguard came too. The lifeguard climbed up a tall white chair and sat down high above the water.

"Why do you sit up there?" Parker asked.

"So I can watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it," she said.

Parker splashed his feet in the cool water. He chased a leaf with his toes. Then his friend Ben slipped on the wet step. Ben went under with a splash.

The lifeguard blew her whistle. She jumped down fast. She lifted Ben up and out of the water. Ben coughed one little cough.

"I saw you from up high," she said. "I saw you right away."

Parker looked up at the tall chair. He waved his hand. The lifeguard waved back.

After swim time, Mom called everyone to lunch under the shady tree. Parker ate his sandwich and looked at the tall chair again. The lifeguard gave him a big smile and a thumbs up.

Bennett stood by his window. "Can we go to Mia's house now?" he asked. Mama shook her head. "Not now, sweet boy. We go tomorrow." Bennett frowned. He wanted the round swing in Mia's yard. He would miss it if he stayed home.

"Is tomorrow now?" Bennett asked. "No," said Mama. "Tomorrow is the day after today. First we sleep. Then it is tomorrow." Bennett looked at the sky. "Sleep first?" he asked. "Sleep first," said Mama.

Bennett put on his pajamas. He hugged his bear. He got into his little bed. "Now I sleep," he said. "Then tomorrow comes." Mama kissed his head. "Yes. Sleep now. Fun later." Bennett closed his eyes.

The sun came up. Bennett opened his eyes. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked. Mama smiled. "It is tomorrow! It is the day after today." Bennett jumped up. "Now we go to Mia's house now!" He found his shoes. He held the door handle. "Mia! I am coming!" he called. Mama laughed. "Let's go, Bennett. Let's go."

Jordan put three carrot seeds in a deep hole. He patted the dirt down soft. Then he filled his little watering can. He gave the seeds a drink of water.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He saw only dirt. "Where is my sprout?" he said. His teacher smiled. "Give it more water," she said. "It is not ready yet."

So Jordan watered the seeds every day. He made a circle of small stones around the spot. He shared his watering can with his friend Milo too.

One morning, Jordan saw something green. A tiny sprout was peeking up. "Milo, come look!" he called. Milo ran over fast. They bent down low. The sprout waved in the wind. Jordan whispered, "Hello, little sprout."

Audrey was in the playroom with her toy ducks. One duck, two ducks, three yellow ducks. Her friends Ben and Mia came in. "Let's play Duck Race," said Mia. Audrey knew this game. Everyone lines up the ducks. Then everyone counts to three. Then everyone pushes a duck to the wall. Mom sat by the door, folding slow, warm towels.

The first race started. "One, two three, go!" The ducks slid on the soft rug. Mia's duck won. "Hooray, Mia!" said Audrey. They played again. This time Ben's duck won. Then came the third race. Audrey's duck was winning. But Mia picked up her duck and moved it. "Now my duck is at the wall," said Mia. "I win."

Ben put his duck down. "That's not the game," he said. Audrey put her duck down too. She did not want to play like that. Nobody pushed any more ducks. The rug was quiet. Mia's face went hot and red. A box of crayons tipped over and the crayons began to spill out, but Mom came over slow and caught them.

"Feeling sad, Mia?" Mom asked. Mia nodded. Audrey held out her hand. "Want to try again? We all follow the same game," said Audrey. Mia wiped her eyes. "Okay. Same game." They lined up the ducks. One duck, two ducks, three yellow ducks. "One, two, three, go!" This time nobody moved a duck. Ben's duck won fair and square. Everybody clapped, even Audrey, even Mia.

Mom gave out apple slices. They were sweet and crunchy. Audrey took her slice and sat close to Mia. "Good game," said Mia. Audrey smiled and patted her yellow duck. "Same game tomorrow?" said Audrey. "Same game tomorrow," said Mia, and they bumped their apple slices together.

Logan ran into the baby store. "A baby is coming!" he said. "We need tiny socks, Mommy!" Mommy smiled. Logan followed her down the big aisle.

Then Logan saw a baby doll in a crib. He patted it hard. Bump! The doll's head fell over. Logan frowned. A lady who worked there came close. "A new baby must be touched very gently," she said. Logan looked at his hand.

He tried again. He stroked the doll's soft hand, slow and light. The doll stayed still. "I did it!" said Logan. Then the doll made a tiny sound, "Wah!" Logan jumped. "Mommy, the baby talks!" He picked cozy blue socks for the real baby. "Come on, baby brother," he whispered. "Hurry to my house!"

Eleanor was so excited. Tonight was Diwali night! Mama gave her a basket of little clay lamps. "These are called diyas," said Mama.

Eleanor set them out in a row. One, two, three, four, five. They were cool and smooth to touch. "Why are they dark?" Eleanor asked. "Watch Papa," said Mama.

Papa came with a long match. He did not let Eleanor touch the flame. He tipped the flame into each little diya. One, two, three, four, five. Each one glowed! The dark lamps turned into golden lights, one by one.

"Wow!" said Eleanor. "The flame makes them bright!" Papa smiled. The diyas sat in a shiny row on the messy table. Together they lit up the whole night. Eleanor clapped her hands. "More diyas next year!"

Luna ran up to the bookmobile. The shelves were full of books. She picked one about a little red fox. "This one," she said. The librarian smiled. "Would you like your very own library card?" Luna nodded and nodded. She got a small card with her name on it. It felt like a gift.

The librarian stamped the book. "This is the due date," she said. "The book has to come back by that day." Luna held the fox book tight. She did not want to give it back, not ever. At home, she read it many times. But when the day came, Mom said, "Time to move the fox book into our bag." Luna frowned. "Will the shelf be empty without it?" she asked. "No," said Mom. "Another kid will read it next."

Luna carried the book to the bookmobile. She put it right on the shelf. Then she found a new book about a big yellow moon. The librarian stamped it. Luna hugged it and waved goodbye to the little red fox.

Ellie ran to the white ball on the grass. It was soccer day at the park. Her coach was there. Her mom was there too.

Ellie kicked the ball. Then a boy on her team kicked it into the net. Everyone cheered. But a man in a striped shirt blew his whistle. He shook his head. The boy yelled, "No! We want the point!"

Ellie felt worried. She asked her coach, "Who is that man?"

The coach said, "He is the referee." Ellie waited. The coach said more. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules."

Ellie looked at the referee. He pointed to a line on the grass. The ball had gone past the line. That was why he blew the whistle.

The game went on. Ellie kicked the ball to her friend. Her friend kicked it into the net. This time the referee clapped his hands. "Good goal!" he said.

The team did not win the game. But they got juice boxes after. Ellie sat with her mom by the gate. She waved to the referee. He waved back.

Aiden was at the big hall with Grandma. Everyone was making food. Soon they would all eat together.

Grandma held Aiden's hands. "In Japan, we say itadakimasu before we eat," she said. "It gives thanks for the food."

Aiden wanted to say it just right. He tried. "Ita... ducky... moose!"

Grandma laughed. "Almost! Try again."

"Ita-daki-masu," said Grandma, slow and slow.

Aiden puffed out his chest. "Ita-daki-masu!"

"That's it!" said Grandma. "Say it loud so the whole table hears."

The food came out. The bowls were big and warm. Aiden waited. He did not grab the bread. He had big eyes and a big want.

"Now, Aiden," said Grandma.

"Itadakimasu!" said Aiden.

"Itadakimasu!" said everyone back.

Then they all ate. Aiden took a big bite of rice. "Mmm," he said. "Is it true? The word tastes good too?"

Grandma smiled. "Words don't taste, silly."

Aiden giggled. "My tummy says thank you."

"My tummy too," said Grandma.

After the meal, Aiden put on his red boot. Then he lost the other one. "I need my boot!" he said.

"It's under the table," said Grandma.

Aiden reached down. He pulled it out. "Found you, boot!"

He pushed his feet in and stomped. "Ita-daki-stomp!"

Grandda laughed big. "You are a silly one."

At the door, Aiden waved. "Bye, hall! Bye, food!"

Grandma took his hand. "Say it one more time for the walk home."

"Itadakimasu!" Aiden shouted.

A bird flew up off the fence.

"Look," said Aiden. "The bird heard me!"

Eliana sat in her car seat. "Are we going to the park?" she asked. "Not today," said Mama. "We are going to the dentist. He will look at your teeth." Eliana made a funny face. "How can he see inside my mouth?" she asked. "It is dark in there, like a little cave." Mama smiled and kept driving.

At the dentist's office, Eliana climbed up into a big chair. It went up and up, like a ride. The dentist leaned over. "Open wide," he said. Eliana opened her mouth. Then a bright light came on above the chair. Eliana squeezed her eyes shut. "Too sunny!" she said. The light made her squint, like when she looked at the sky.

The dentist handed her little sunglasses. "Try these," he said. Eliana put them on. Now she could keep her eyes open. The bright light shone down above the chair, right into her open mouth. "I can see every tooth," said the dentist. "So that is what the light is for," thought Eliana. The dentist counted her teeth, one, two, three.

After that, they got a snack. Eliana was hungry. She ate a crunchy apple. It tasted sweet. "No dirt on this apple," said Mama with a laugh. "The dentist likes clean teeth." Eliana smiled her biggest smile. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked.

Mila found her toy cat on the rug. The cat had a long tail and a short tail, because there were two cats. "Which one is big?" she asked. Mom smiled. "The gray one is big. The white one is small."

Mila wanted to give the cats water. She carried a little cup. She walked fast, then slow. Oh no. The water jumped out. It made a puddle on the floor. Mila stepped in it. Her socks got wet. "My socks are wet," she said. "I need dry socks." Mom brought new ones. "Wet and dry are opposites," said Mom. Mila touched the wet sock, then the dry sock. They did not feel the same.

Mom made warm milk after. It was hot, so Mom held the cup. Mila waited until it was cold. She took a little sip. "Cold now," she said. The big cat got a dry spot in the sun. The small cat sat by the door. "Sleep well, cats," said Mila. She patted the long tail, soft and slow.

Noah ran into the backyard. His team was waiting on the grass. All the kids had green shirts on. Noah had a green shirt too.

The coach blew the whistle. "Pass the ball," she said. Noah kicked the ball to a boy. But the boy had a blue shirt. The blue boy ran away with the ball. Noah stood still. He had given the ball away.

"Look for green shirts," said his friend Mia. Noah looked around. He saw green shirts here and there. Mia waved her arms. Her green shirt was bright in the sun. Noah kicked the ball to Mia. Mia kicked it back. The green team cheered.

After the game, Noah sat on the grass. He patted the ball like a horse going slow. "Good ball," he said. "Next time I will guess right. I will look for green." A bee buzzed by the fence. It was getting late. Dad called from the porch, "Time for dinner, Noah." Noah picked up the ball and ran home across the soft green grass.

Elijah put on his skates at the ice rink. The ice looked fresh and shiny. But first, Dad said, they would watch the big game. It was on the big screen above the snack bar. Mom, Grandpa, and his friend Mia sat on the long bench with him.

The players ran fast up and down the court. Elijah watched the ball go in the hoop. The people around him clapped and cheered. "Go, go!" Elijah shouted. His eye followed the ball the whole way.

Then a loud sound came from the game. Tweet! All the players stopped running. They stood still on the court. Elijah tugged Dad's sleeve. "Why did they stop?" he asked. Dad pointed at the man in the striped shirt. "That is the referee," Dad said. "The referee blows a whistle to stop play." The referee held the little whistle up to his mouth.

Elijah waited. The game started again. The players ran once more. Then, tweet! The whistle blew again. The players stopped again. Elijah laughed. He clapped his mittens together. "They stopped again!" he said. Mom gave his cold cheek a kiss. Then Elijah took Dad's hand and stepped out onto the fresh ice.

Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted red apples. He held Mama's hand in the middle of the big aisle. A girl stood by the apples with her dad. "I went to the park tomorrow," she said. Then she shook her head. "No, not tomorrow. Yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." Theodore looked up. He saw the apples. He kicked his shoe softly on the floor. "Mama, we got apples yesterday," he said. "That was yesterday," said Mama. "Today we get more." "And tomorrow we eat them," said Theodore. "Yes," said Mama. "Tomorrow." She put three red apples in the bag. One apple sat in the dark bottom of the cart. "Can we eat one now?" asked Theodore. "Not now," said Mama. "Later, at home." At home, later came. Mama cut the apples. Theodore sat close and waited. "Tomorrow we get more," he said. Mama smiled and handed him a slice. "Tomorrow," she said.

Margot sat on her bed. She had a big crayon and one piece of paper. She wanted to write a note to Grandpa.

She wrote: ILOVEYOUGRANDPA. All the letters ran together in one long line. "Look, Bunny!" she said. "One, two, three, four letters. More letters. More letters. All in a big hug!"

Grandpa came in. He held the paper. He turned it around. He looked and looked. "Hmm," he said. "Is it a secret code?"

Margot frowned. "It says I love you, Grandpa!"

Grandpa smiled. "I need a space between the words. One word, then a little space, then the next word."

Margot made tiny dots with her crayon. Pop, pop, pop. One space. Two spaces. Three spaces. Now the note said: I LOVE YOU GRANDPA.

Grandpa read it out loud. He gave Margot a big hug. "Best note ever," he said.

Then Margot found her stinky sock under the bed. She dropped it in the basket. "Even socks go in their own space," she said. Grandpa laughed and laughed.

Sophie sits in the car. The baby sits in his little seat. He is coming home today.

Sophie counts the things in the car. One blue bag. Two blankets. Three baby socks. All the things are for the baby.

Sophie has no things. "Mom," she says. "I miss you. It was just you and me before." Mom turns around in her seat. "I miss that too," Mom says. "It is okay to feel left out, Sophie. Big sisters can feel that way."

Mom holds out her hand. Sophie holds it. Mom's hand is warm. Then the baby makes a small sound. His face goes deep red. He is hungry.

Dad stops the car. Mom feeds the baby. Sophie waits. Then Mom says, "One cookie for my big girl." Sophie takes a bite. The baby watches her with big eyes.

"Hello, baby," says Sophie. "This is my cookie. I will share."

Parker wanted to paint at school. But the paint cups were missing. "They are drying," said Miss Ana. "We washed them yesterday. They will be dry today."

Parker looked at the big clock on the wall. "When will it be time to paint?" he asked. Miss Ana pointed at the clock. "The clock shows what time it is," she said. "The little hand moves. When it points up, it will be paint time."

Parker watched the clock. He stacked blocks. He looked again. The hand moved a tiny bit. He read a book about a bear. He looked up. The hand moved some more.

"Now!" called Miss Ana. The paint cups were dry. Parker dipped his brush in red. He made a big sun. "Tomorrow," he said, "I will paint a moon."

Luka sat at the paint table at summer camp. He had a pot of yellow. He had a pot of blue. He wanted to make green, like the grass.

"Try a little blue first," said his teacher, Mia. Luka dipped his brush. He stirred the blue into all the yellow. Swirl, swirl, swirl. Now the whole pot was green. Luka poked at it with his brush. He tried to find some yellow. It was gone. The blue and the yellow would not come apart again.

Mia smiled. "Next time, keep a little of each aside." She gave him a fresh pot of yellow. Luka kept a small bit safe in a cup. Then he mixed the rest, slow and careful. Green! He laughed. "Mother, look!" he called across the field. "Green like the grass!" His shy friend Pip peeped over and clapped.

Evelyn sat on the red rug. Mama put on a song. The song had a steady beat. Evelyn clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps went with the beat. The dog barked at the music.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat wore a big hat." Evelyn wanted to sing it too. She sang, "The cat wore a big..." Then she stopped. She forgot the last word. She looked down at her block tower.

"What rhymes with cat?" asked Mama. Evelyn thought hard. Then she said, "Hat! Cat and hat sound the same!" She sang the whole rhyme. "The cat wore a big hat." She clapped on the beat while she sang.

Daddy came in to listen. Evelyn patted the rug so he could sit. She sang it again, all by herself. "The cat wore a big hat!" Then she clapped and clapped. The dog wagged his tail to the beat. Evelyn giggled and sang one more time.

Clara loved her school. There was a big door at the front. There was a small door for the hamster, Nibbles. At snack time, Miss Rosa poured warm milk. "Hot," said Clara, and she blew on it. Then she drank it slow. Slow sips, like a snail.

After lunch, the class had rest time. Clara lay on her mat. She closed her eyes. She counted one, two, three. Then she fell fast asleep, fast like a rabbit running.

Clara woke up. The room was dark. She looked out the window. The sky was dark too. "Is it morning?" she asked. "Is it time to go home?" Miss Rosa sat by her. "It is still night," she said softly. "Day and night are opposites. Night comes after day, and day comes after night." Clara looked at the dark sky. She saw a wild owl fly by. Its wing went whoosh, whoosh. One owl. Two wings.

Clara waited on her mat. She counted one, two, three, four. At last the sky turned light. The room turned bright. Miss Rosa turned on the little lamp. "Now it is day," Clara said. She got up slow, like a snail. She looked at Nibbles. He was awake too. "Good morning, Nibbles," she whispered. "Good morning, day."

Henry put on his red shoe. Then he put on the other one. "We are going on a trip!" he said. The car was packed full of bags. Dad started the engine. Henry sat in his seat and looked out the window.

The sky looked stormy and gray. "Will the rain stop our trip?" Henry asked. "No," said Mom. "We will drive right past it." The rain tapped on the roof. Tap, tap, tap. Then the sun came out. Henry clapped his hands.

Soon they got to the airport. Airports are busy places. Henry saw big planes out the window. He wanted to run to them fast. "Wait," said Mom. She held out her hand. Henry remembered. In busy places, he stays close to his grown-up. He grabbed Mom's hand and held it tight. Together they walked through the crowd.

"Can I see the planes?" asked Henry. "Yes," said Dad. "Hand in hand, all the way." Henry held on. They walked and walked. Then they stopped at a big window. A huge plane zoomed up into the sky. Henry pressed his nose to the glass. "Up, up, up it goes!"

Kinsley went to the park with Dad. She saw a big red ball near the slide. She wanted to play with it. A boy named Tom had the ball. Tom threw the ball to his friend. His friend ran off with it. Then the friend stopped. He turned around and said, "Thank you, Tom!" Then he ran back to play. Kinsley watched with wide eyes.

Kinsley wanted a turn too. She walked to Tom. "Can I have the ball, please?" she asked. Tom smiled and rolled the ball to her. Kinsley caught it. She held it tight. The slide was wet and slippery, so she played on the flat square of pavement instead. She kicked the ball high. It flew over the bench and landed in a bush. Kinsley felt worried. "My ball is stuck," she said. Dad came over. "I can help," he said. Dad reached in and got the ball out.

Kinsley hugged the ball. "Thank you, Dad," she said. Dad smiled. Tom waved from the swings. "Come play!" he called. Kinsley ran to him over the square tiles. She passed the ball to Tom. Tom caught it. "Thank you, Kinsley!" he said. They laughed and kicked the ball back and forth. Dad sat on the bench and watched. The sun went down slow. "Time to cook dinner," said Dad. Kinsley took his hand. "Bye, Tom! Thank you for playing!" she called. Tom waved his big wave.

Axel sat down at the dinner table. He was very hungry. "Peas tonight!" he said. Mama put the plate in front of him.

"Let's count them," said Mama. "One, two, three, four, five." Axel counted five green peas. Then he counted his fingers too. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. "Five fingers, five peas!"

Then Axel saw his birthday card on the table. It had a big red mark on it. The mark looked like this: 5. "What is that?" he asked. "That is five," said Mama. Axel's eyes got wide. "That is my five? The same five?" He held up five fingers next to the card. "Five and five! They match!"

"Now eat your peas," said Mama. "Don't forget your carrots too." Axel ate fast. Then he smiled big. One tooth was missing in front. "I want to count to ten now," he said. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

After dinner, Axel ran to the door. There was a number on it too. He pointed at it and shouted, "That says five too! I found another one!"

Anthony woke up early. "Is today the library day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is today," she said. "Today is the day that is happening right now." Anthony clapped his hands. "Right now! Right now!" he said.

At the library, Anthony picked books. One, two, three books. He heard kids reading. He saw a story time sign. "Can we go now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later, after we find our books." Later came, and they sat in the story circle.

On the way home, Anthony held Mom's hand. "We went to the library yesterday," he said. Mom shook her head. "No, that was today," she said. "Yesterday is all done. Tomorrow is a new day." Anthony thought. "Tomorrow can we go back?" he asked. Mom laughed. "Tomorrow we will bake a cake. You can help. But not now, now we walk home." Anthony smiled. "One, two, three books for today."

Riley wanted to help Grandma feed the hens. "You can toss the corn," said Grandma. "Count the hens so we know they all come."

Riley looked out at the yard. She counted, "One, two, four." Grandma laughed. "You jumped too far! After two comes three. Try again, slow."

Riley took a big breath. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten hens ran to her. Ten hens pecked the corn. "The words fit!" said Riley.

Then Riley saw something silly. A tiny hen hid under a warm blanket by the door. It was very quiet there. "One more makes eleven," said Grandma. Riley giggled. "Silly hen, you missed counting time."

The little hen fluffed her feathers to dry. Riley gave her a small handful of corn. The tiny hen pecked Riley's shoe. "That tickles!" said Riley. Grandma carried the hen back to the yard, and Riley waved. "Bye-bye, number eleven."

Alice sat in her car seat. The sun was warm on her hands. "Are we at Mia's house now?" she asked. "Not now," said Mama. "Today we go to the store. Tomorrow we go to Mia's house." Alice made a sad mouth. "I want to go now," she said. Mama kept driving.

The store had big doors. The doors went whoosh. Alice held Mama's hand. They picked a heavy bag of apples. Alice helped put it in the cart. The apples rolled and bumped. "Mia likes apples," said Alice. "Yes," said Mama. "You can bring some tomorrow."

In the car, the sun began to drop. It made long shadows on the road. Alice yawned. "Is it tomorrow yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "First comes night. You will sleep. When you wake up, that is tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today." Alice looked out the window. The streetlights came on, one by one.

Alice ate an apple in her seat. Her eyes felt heavy. At home, she slept in her little bed. When she woke up, the sun was back. "Is it today again?" she asked. Mama smiled. "It is a new today," she said. "Now it is tomorrow." Alice clapped her hands. "Mia's house!" she said. She put the apples in her small bag, one, two, three.

Owen did not want to go to the doctor. "Shots make me grumpy," he said. Mom laughed. "No shots today. Just a checkup." Owen held his toy bear. The bear needed a checkup too.

First the doctor looked in Owen's ears. "Ears are for hearing," she said. Owen heard the paper crinkle under him. Then she looked in his eyes. "Eyes are for seeing." Owen saw a sticker chart on the wall. He sniffed the air. "This room smells like my bread at home," he said. The doctor laughed. "Your nose knows!"

The doctor held a tiny cup. "Taste this," she said. It was sweet. "Yum," said Owen. "Your tongue did that," she said. Then she put a cotton ball in his hand. "Squeeze it." It was soft and squishy.

"Now take off your shoes and socks," said the doctor. Owen pulled them off. He put his bare toes on the cold floor. "Brrr!" he said. Then the doctor put a soft towel under his feet. His toes felt warm and fuzzy.

"Your feet can feel things too," said the doctor, "like soft grass under bare toes." Owen looked down. He wiggled his toes on the towel. The towel tickled, just like grass!

At home, Mom let Owen play in the yard. He took off his shoes again. He stepped on the green grass. "Tickle, tickle, toes!" he shouted. Then Owen put his bear in the grass. "You can feel it too," he told the bear. He ran in a circle, laughing. "My feet are so smart!"

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Olivier was so happy. On day one, they went to the big park. Grandpa sat on the green bench. He opened his bag. He took out bread. "This is my bread," said Grandpa. "Our family has made it for a long, long time. My own grandma taught me."

Olivier took a little bite. It was warm inside. How did it get so soft? "Can I help make it?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandpa. "We will cook it together tomorrow."

The next morning, they stood in the kitchen. Grandpa gave Olivier a bowl. Olivier put in flour. Grandpa poured the water. Olivier mixed it with a spoon. The dough was sticky and stiff.

Then Grandpa said, "Now we push it and fold it." Olivier pushed the dough. He folded it. He pushed it again. The dough began to feel different. It became soft and stretchy! "Look, Grandpa! My hands did that!" said Olivier.

Grandpa put the dough near the warm oven, where grown-ups watch. They waited. The dough got big and puffy. Grandpa slid it in with his big gloves. Soon the kitchen smelled wonderful.

At the park, they sat by the pond. A sign said, "Feed the ducks, not the geese." Olivier laughed. He held his warm slice of family bread. He took a big bite and said, "Grandpa, can we make it again tomorrow?"

Emmett ran into the kitchen. He smelled something sweet. Mom was baking. "Blueberries!" he said. His nose knew.

Then Dad turned on the blender. It roared. It was so loud! Emmett jumped. "Too loud!" he said. He put his hands over his ears. The roar got smaller. The blender went on and on. Then Dad turned it off. Quiet! Emmett took his hands off his ears.

"How did it get quiet so fast?" he asked. "I covered my ears," he said. "My hands made the loud sound little!" He tried again. He clapped his hands over his ears. "Quiet, quiet, quiet," he whispered. He lifted them. He could hear Mom humming. Down came the hands. Quiet again!

"Can you help me?" asked Mom. Emmett looked at the blueberries. He touched one. It was cold and smooth. He tasted one. Sweet! "Yum," said Dad, tasting one too.

After his nap, Emmett heard the vacuum. It was loud and wild. He covered his ears with both hands. The vacuum sound got little. Then Mom began to sweep the floor. The broom went swish, swish. That sound was soft. Emmett took his hands down.

"I have two ears, two eyes, one nose, one tongue, and two hands," he counted. "That is me!"

"And me," said Dad, and he tickled Emmett's tummy. Emmett laughed out loud.

Jasmine sat at her little table. She was drawing a picture. It was a picture of a party. A party in the grass, with cake and balloons.

Jasmine picked up a gray crayon. She wanted to draw the sky. Then she looked up at the window. The sun was shining big and bright. It was a sunny day. There was not one cloud. And the sky over the roofs was blue. Bright, bright blue.

Jasmine put the gray crayon down. She picked up the blue crayon instead. She drew the sky all blue, up and up and up. "Blue," she said. "Blue, blue, blue." She drew a yellow sun too. Then she drew red balloons. Then she drew green grass for the party.

Jasmine was hungry after all that drawing. Mommy called, "Snack time!" Jasmine marched to the kitchen with her picture. She held it up high. Mommy looked at the blue sky and smiled. "What a sunny day," said Mommy. Jasmine sat down and took a big bite of her apple. Outside the window, the sky stayed blue.

Felix went to the band room with his class. He saw a big drum and a small bell. He wanted to play the bell. "May I try?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "Take your time."

On the stand there was a paper. It had little dots and lines on it. "What are those dots?" Felix asked. Miss Ana smiled. "Those marks are called notes," she said. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Felix looked closely. He tapped the bell where the dots sat. Ding! He tapped again. Ding, ding! A bird sat by the window. It sang along. The notes climbed up the page, and Felix tapped higher sounds. Ding, ding, ding!

One dot looked tricky. Felix tapped the wrong spot. The sound was too low. He was a little upset. He took a breath. He waited. Then he found the right dot. Ding! The bird sang louder. "Again," said Felix. Ding, ding, ding!

Cooper put on his warm coat. Off to the ice rink! Mom and Dad came too. Grandma came too. Even his best friend Ruby came.

The players zoomed on the ice. Their helmets were blue and red. But one man had a striped shirt. He was not on a team. Cooper pointed. "Who is that?" he asked. Dad smiled. "That is the referee," he said. Cooper watched the referee. The referee watched the game. He watched and watched and watched.

Then a blue player pushed a red player. He pushed him right down! The referee blew his whistle. Toot! He held up his arm. The blue player had to sit down. Cooper jumped up and down. "The referee saw it! The referee saw it!" he shouted. Ruby clapped her hands.

After the game, they ate warm pretzels. Cooper held up his arm like the referee. Toot, he said, and laughed. "When I grow big, I will watch the game too. I will be the referee!" Grandma hugged him tight. "Best referee ever," she said.

Ruby went to the doctor with her mama. "The doctor will look at you," Mama said. "And I get a sticker after!" said Ruby.

First the doctor looked in Ruby's ears. "You hear with your ears," said the doctor. He rang a little bell. Ding, ding! Ruby heard it with her ears. Then he looked in Ruby's eyes. Ruby saw the light. It was bright! Then Ruby opened her mouth. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Ruby smelled the sticker sheet on his desk. It smelled like strawberries! The doctor touched Ruby's neck. His fingers were warm.

Then the doctor held out an ice cube. "You can touch it," he said. Ruby touched the ice cube. It felt cold! Ruby pulled her hand back fast. "Cold!" she laughed. She touched it again and giggled. Then the doctor said, "All done. What do we do now?" Ruby shouted, "Sticker time!" She picked a shiny red heart and stuck it on her hand.

Jacob skipped into the kitchen. The table smelled like warm bread. Grandma was setting out bowls. Jacob clapped his hands.

"Soup night!" said Grandma. "First we say the blessing."

Jacob wanted to say it too. He wanted it so much. But he did not know how.

"Watch us," said Grandma. "Then you try."

Daddy stood by the table. Daddy closed his eyes. Daddy bowed his head. Grandpa did it too. His eyes closed. His head went down.

Jacob peeked. One eye open. He saw Grandpa's head bowed low. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut tight. Jacob closed his eye fast.

Grandma said the blessing. Her voice was soft like snow falling.

Now it was Jacob's turn. He squeezed his eyes shut. He bent his little head way down. "Thank you for the soup," he said. "Thank you for Grandma. Thank you for Grandpa. Thank you for Daddy. One, two, three, four!"

Nobody laughed at him. Everybody smiled.

"Jacob said it!" said Grandma.

"Jacob said the whole blessing," said Grandpa.

Jacob looked up. His eyes opened wide. "Again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. "Every soup night."

Jacob sat up tall and picked up his spoon. "I love soup nights," he said.

Florence stood in the backyard with her red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop. Her big brother Sam held the hoop up low. Florence threw the beanbag. It fell on the grass. "Try again," said Sam. Florence picked it up. She threw it slowly this time. The beanbag went into the hoop. "Yay!" said Florence. She jumped up and down.

Then Sam brought out a big yellow ball. "Now catch," he said. He rolled it to her gently. Florence held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers. It rolled away under the tree. Florence ran after it. She tried one hand again. The ball fell again.

Sam sat down on the grass. "The wind can blow the ball," he said. "Want to try more?" Florence nodded. This time she held out both hands. She made a big round circle with her arms. Sam rolled the ball. Florence caught it! She did not drop it. "I got it!" she said.

Sam clapped. Their dog Rex woke up from being asleep by the fence. Rex ran over and barked at the ball. Florence laughed. She threw the ball high in the air. It landed right on Rex's head. Rex thought it was a new game. He pushed the ball back to Florence with his nose. Florence got ready with both hands.

Muffins were baking in the oven. Carter wanted to see them. He started to reach for the oven door. "Stop," said Mom. "It is hot." Mom held his hand. They stood back and watched together. The oven light glowed. Warm air moved out of the top. "Where is the cold spot?" Carter wondered. He found it by the door. It felt nice there.

Carter looked out the window. His big sister Lily was on the playground slide. She climbed up, up, up. Then she lay down on her tummy, head first. Carter tapped the glass. Lily sat up. She turned herself around. Her feet pointed down the slide. Whoosh! She went down feet first and landed on her feet.

"Did you see that?" said Carter. Mom smiled. The timer rang. The muffins were done. Mom used her big mitts to move the pan out. Carter smelled them from his safe, cold spot by the door. Then he and Mom sat down, and each ate one warm muffin.

Jules was hungry. He wanted bread with honey. Mama got the bread from the top of the shelf. She cut it with the knife. Jules watched from his stool, far away.

The bread went in the toaster. Ping! It popped up. Jules heard the pop with his ears. "The toast is ready!" said Mama. Jules touched the plate. It was warm. His fingers could feel warm.

Jules sniffed the toast with his nose. "Mmm, it smells good," he said. "Where does the smell go in?" Mama smiled. "Your nose has two little openings. They are called nostrils." Jules touched his nose. He felt two soft holes, one and then two.

Jules ran to the mirror. He looked with his eyes. He counted. "One, two! I see my nostrils!" He sniffed again. Sniff, sniff. Could he smell with just one? He covered one nostril. The smell was small. He let go. The smell was big again!

He licked the honey toast with his tongue. Sweet! "Is it too late for more toast?" he asked. "No," said Mama, laughing. She dropped in two more slices. Jules knocked on the counter. Knock, knock, knock. Ping! The toast jumped up high, right past the top of the toaster.

Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. Teacher Anna held up a big card with words. "This is a recipe," she said. "It tells us what to use and what to do, one step at a time."

Max looked at the recipe. Flour, eggs, milk. One cup, two cups, stir, stir. But Max was so excited that he skipped the eggs. He just stirred the flour and milk. His tummy rumbled. Pancakes, pancakes, soon!

Teacher Anna poured the batter onto the pan. Flip, flip. But Max's pancake came out flat. Flat as a rain puddle! Papa giggled. Mama giggled. "Oh no," said Max. "My pancake is sad."

"Let's read the recipe again," said Teacher Anna. They read it one step at a time. Flour, then eggs, then milk. Max cracked the eggs himself. Stir, stir, stir. This time the pancake puffed up big and round. "It's a happy pancake!" said Max. Papa took a big bite. "Mmm," he said. "One more, please!"

Edouard ran into the playroom. He clapped his hands. "Monkey time!" he shouted. He tipped out his toy box. Ten little monkeys fell out on the soft rug.

He lined up five monkeys on the bed. He counted them. "One, two, three, four, five!" Then he began to sing. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

He bumped one monkey onto the floor. The monkey sat in a bit of dirt by the rug. "Now four!" said Edouard. He sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" He bumped one more off. "Now three!"

One monkey was alone on the floor. Edouard giggled. It was Mama's turn next. She came in and sang the last part with him. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!"

Edouard hugged all the monkeys. "Let's do it again!"

Brielle got to school early. Teacher Mia put a pencil on her desk. "You can write your name," said Teacher Mia.

Brielle picked up the pencil. She held it tight and walked to the table. The point was up in the air. It waved near Leo's arm. "Careful," said Teacher Mia. "Carry a pencil with the point facing down."

Brielle turned the pencil around. The point went down, near the floor. She walked all the way to her chair. Nobody got poked. Then she held the pencil the way Teacher Mia showed her. She made a B. She made an R. Her letters were wiggly, but they were her letters. "Look, I wrote Brielle!" she said. Leo clapped for her.

Kinsley wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. She got her paper and her blue paint. She sat close to Mama at the big table. Mama had a hot mug of cocoa. "Mine is hot," said Mama. "Yours is cold milk." Kinsley touched her own cup. It felt cool and nice.

Then Kinsley dropped her paint brush. It rolled away. It rolled behind the couch. Kinsley went to get it. She looked behind the couch. She saw a little box with holes in the wall. It was an outlet. Her fingers wiggled toward it.

Kinsley stopped. She did not touch it. She ran back to Mama. "There are holes in the wall," she said. "Behind the couch." Mama came right away. "That is an outlet," said Mama. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet. I will get your brush." Mama reached with a grown-up hand and got the brush out.

Kinsley sat down again. She painted big white flakes. "It looks like snow," said Mama. Kinsley smiled. "That is true," she said. "It snows at Grandma's house." She stayed right by Mama and painted until the whole page was full.

Arnaud ran to the story corner. He saw the big red robot book on the shelf. He wanted it now.

"Can we read the robot book now?" he asked.

Teacher Mia smiled. "Not now. Story time is after snack."

"But I want it now," said Arnaud.

"Now means at this very moment," said Teacher Mia. "Now we wash hands. Later we eat. Then the story comes."

Arnaud looked at the clock. He heard the water run. He filled his hands with soap bubbles. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop.

At the table, Arnaud ate his crackers. He heard a loud bell ring. That was the end of snack!

"Now?" he asked Teacher Mia.

"Now," she said.

Arnaud clapped. Yesterday the robot book was on the shelf all day. Today he waited, and then it happened. Tomorrow he would pick it first again.

Teacher Mia opened the book. The robot on the first page beeped hello.

"Hello, robot," said Arnaud.

Lucy ran into the playroom. "Look, Teddy!" she said. "A big slide!" The slide was tall. Beside it sat a small red slide for the dolls. Lucy put her friend Teddy at the top of the big slide. "You go first!" she said.

Lucy climbed up. She went up and up, one step, two steps, three steps. Then she sat at the top. "Wheee!" She slid down, fast. Teddy slid down too. "Fast!" laughed Lucy. Then she climbed up again. This time she went down very, very slow, like a sleepy snail. Mom brought warm cocoa. "Careful, it's hot," said Mom. Mom held the cup so nothing would spill. Lucy blew on it. "Now it's cold!" she said, opening her eyes wide.

"Up and down are opposites," said Mom. Lucy looked at the slide. She climbed up. She came down. Up, then down. She tried it again and again. "Teddy, watch me!" she called. She went up the ladder and slid down, fast, fast, fast.

Sarah was at Grandma's house. Ten red apples sat in a big bowl. Sarah wanted to count them all by herself.

She started at the left side. One, two, three. She went slowly. Four, five, six. Grandma waited. Seven, eight, nine, ten. "Ten apples!" said Sarah.

Grandma poured milk into two cups. "Now let's count them again," she said. "Start at the other end this time."

Sarah started at the right side. One, two, three. She took her time. The cat watched from the chair. Four, five, six. Seven, eight, nine, ten.

Sarah put her hands on her cheeks. "Ten again! Ten both ways!" Grandma smiled and put one apple in each cup. "Ten again," said Sarah.

Then Grandma held up two plates. Cookies on one. Crackers on the other. "Which plate has more?"

Sarah counted the cookies. One, two, three, four, five. She counted the crackers. One, two, three. "The cookies!" she said. "The cookies have more!"

Grandma gave her a cookie. The dirty bowl went to the sink. Sarah ate her cookie and counted her bites. One, two, three. She laughed. "I can count anything!"

Violet got to daycare. Her coat was cold from outside. She hung it on her hook. Teacher Mia said, "Snack time is soon." Violet sat down at the little table. She waited. Soon means in a little while, said her friend Ben. Violet tapped her feet. She looked out the window. A bird flew by. Then Teacher Mia rang the bell. Snack time came. It did not take long. Violet got a cup. Teacher Mia poured the milk for her. Violet ate her crackers. Yesterday, she had apples at snack. Today, she had crackers. Tomorrow, Teacher Mia said there would be bananas. After snack, the class went outside to paint. Violet painted a big red circle. "It has to dry," said Teacher Mia. "You can take it home later." Violet played in the sand while she waited. She poured sand from one cup to another. The wind blew a little. Then Teacher Mia called, "Paintings are dry now." Violet ran over. Her red circle was dry and shiny. She held it up. "Now I can take it home," she said. She carried it carefully to her hook, and put it in her cubby for later.

Paisley put on her little apron. The chef said, "You can wear it today." In the restaurant kitchen, the toast was ready. A grown-up had made it warm.

Paisley wanted to butter the toast all by herself. She took the knife. It was a safe, soft knife. She dipped it in the butter. She spread the butter on the warm toast. The butter went shiny. Then it melted away. Paisley looked and looked. "My butter is lost!" she said. The chef smiled. "Look again," he said. Paisley tipped the toast to the light. The butter was still there. It was shiny and wet and soft. Warm toast made the butter melt.

Next came the milk. Paisley held the cup with two hands. She poured slow, slow, slow. One drip ran down the side. But the cup did not spill over. "I did it!" said Paisley. The chef clapped his hands.

Outside the window, a tree moved in the wind. Paisley ate her warm, shiny toast. "More milk, please," she said.

Josephine wanted to make a bed for the class bunny. She found a big box on the shelf. She pulled it. The box did not move. She pulled again. Still it stayed. "This box is heavy," said Ben. "It is too heavy for me."

Miss Dana came to help. "Heavy and light are opposites," she said. Together they pushed the big box down. It went slow, slow, slow. Then Josephine found a small pillow. It was light! She lifted it up high. She carried it fast across the room. She put it in the box so the bunny could sleep.

At snack time, Josephine drank cold milk. She touched the warm cup with her hands. The bunny snuggled into the pillow bed. Josephine gave the bunny a soft kiss on its head. "Sleep tight," she said.

Audrey sat in the school library. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write her name.

She wrote the A. She wrote the U. Then she came to the K. She drew it, but it looked wrong. The K was backwards. She tried again. It was still backwards. Her pencil was stuck in her hand, and she wanted to cry.

The teacher came over. She gave Audrey a card. The card had a big K on it. The K was bumpy. "Trace it with your finger," said the teacher. Audrey did. She moved her finger down the K. Then she moved her finger up and out, on both sides. She traced it again and again.

Then Audrey picked up her pencil. She wrote the K. It was right! She wrote her whole name: A-U-D-R-E-Y. Audrey held up her paper and smiled. "I did it!" she said, and she gave the teacher a big hug with both arms.

Rehmat wanted to play the new game. Papa said, "I say a word. You shout its opposite. Opposites are two words that mean things as different as they can be." Rehmat nodded. Papa said, "Big." Rehmat looked around. She pointed at the big teddy bear. Then she held up her small duck. "Small!" she shouted. Papa laughed. Next Papa said, "Fast." Rehmat ran fast across the playroom. Then she walked slow, slow, slow. "Slow!" she said. Papa gave her warm milk. He held the hot cup himself. Rehmat touched her own cool cup. "Cold," she said, and took a sip. Then Papa said a tricky one. He said, "Happy." Rehmat thought hard. She made a grumpy face like her letter blocks had fallen down. Then she smiled big. "Grumpy's opposite is happy, so happy's opposite is grumpy!" Papa clapped. Rehmat gave him a hug. "Again," she said. "Say one more."

Bennett ran into the music room. He wanted to clap and sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by himself. He tried it fast. He tried it slow. His claps went everywhere. The song went one way. His hands went another way. It did not sound right at all.

Miss Rosa sat down next to him. "Try this," she said. "Clap at the same time as the beat." Bennett put down his yellow cup of milk. He hid his hands under his legs and listened first. The song went clap, clap, clap. Then he let his hands out. He clapped when the song clapped. His hands and the music landed together, like two friends jumping at the same time.

"Now the song!" said Miss Rosa. Bennett sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He did not stop clapping. Miss Rosa clapped too. Then everyone in the room clapped with them, all at the same time. Bennett sang louder. "How I wonder what you are!"

Evan ran to Grandma's house. On the wall hung big letters. A, B, C, all the way to Z. "I know that one!" said Evan. "A!"

Then Grandma opened a book. Evan looked at the page. He saw a little round shape. It looked new. It looked shy, hiding in the corner.

"That is not A," said Evan. "That is a different letter!"

Grandma smiled. "That is the same A," she said. "It is a small letter."

"Big A, small a," said Evan. "Same letter!"

"Yes!" said Grandma. "Letters can be big or small."

Evan jumped up and down. He said the letter sound. "Ah, ah, ah!" A feather drifted off the shelf. It made Evan giggle.

"Now the B!" said Evan. He began to climb onto the chair.

"Wait, I will hold you," said Grandma. She held his hand.

"B!" said Evan. "Big B, small b, same letter, buh, buh, buh!"

Grandma laughed. "My smart boy."

Matthew held his mama's hand. The bookmobile was big and blue. It had wheels like a truck.

Inside, a lady smiled at Matthew. "Hello! Are you here for a library card?" Matthew nodded. He wanted a card so much. The lady typed on her computer. Then she gave him a little card with his name on it. Matthew picked a book about a red truck.

The next week, they went back. "Time to bring your book back," said Mama. Matthew hugged the book tight. "My book," he said. He did not want to let it go.

Mama pointed to a small door on the side of the bookmobile. "That is the return slot," she said. "We drop books there to bring them back." Matthew looked at the little door. He pushed his book in. The book slid down, out of sight.

Matthew felt his eyes get hot. Then he heard a soft thump inside. The lady opened the door from the inside. She held up his book! "Here it is, safe and sound," she said. Matthew laughed. The slot had taken the book to her!

He waved at the book. "Bye bye, truck book!" he sang. Then he picked a new one, about a big yellow bus. His smile was loose and happy all the way home.

Sarah ran to the library play corner. There was a big red basket. There were tiny shirts in it. There were tiny socks in it. There was a tiny hat, too.

"Those are all clothes," said Miss Jo. "Clothes go in the basket."

Sarah grabbed the sock. She put it with the toy animals. She put it with the toy cars. Then she laughed and picked it up again. She dropped it in the basket with the shirt and the hat. All the clothes were together now.

Then Sarah found a book with a big picture of a puppy. The puppy had a rough, scratchy coat. Sarah could almost bend the soft page as she turned it.

"Again!" said Sarah. She pulled the clothes out one by one. Shirt. Sock. Hat. Then she sorted them all back in.

"Look, Miss Jo! Clothes!"

Miss Jo clapped. "Good sorting, Sarah."

Sarah hugged the book and grinned. "Puppy next!"

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All clean," he said. "Now you can pick a sticker and a snack."

Grace chose a red sticker. Then she saw apple slices on a tray. Her tummy made a hungry sound. "Wash your hands first," said the nurse. "Use soap. Wash for twenty seconds. That is a long wash."

Grace ran to the little sink. She made bubbles fast. She rinsed fast. "Done!" she said. The nurse shook her head. "That was too quick," she said. Grace frowned. Twenty seconds felt so long. How would she know?

Then Grace remembered camp. At camp they sang a song at the sink. The nurse smiled. "Sing it," she said. Grace sang while she scrubbed. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She scrubbed and sang. The song helped her keep going. When the song ended, she was done.

"Twenty seconds!" said the nurse. Grace looked at her hands. The bubbles had washed away. Where did the sticky jam hide? It was gone now. "My hands feel fuzzy clean," Grace said. She took an apple slice and crunched it. "Can we sing the song at home too?" she asked. "Every time," said Mom. Grace skipped to the door, still humming.

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big pencil in his hand. He wanted to write his name, all by himself. But the pencil wiggled and slipped. His M looked like a wiggly worm.

"I can't do it," said Max. His little brother was too young to write, but he watched from his high chair. Grandma put a paper in front of Max. The letters M, A and X were on it. But they were made of little dots. "Now trace the dots," said Grandma.

Max pressed the pencil down. He went dot to dot to dot. The dots made a big M. He traced again and again. Soon his hand felt steady. Then he tried a letter with no dots at all. It was an A. It came out just right.

"My turn," said Max. He wrote M, A, X on a clean paper. The pencil marks shined, wet and new. "Wait for them to dry," said Grandma. Max watched the shiny lines fade to soft gray. He held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma! That's my name!"

Zoe sat at the paint table. She wanted to make a green leaf for her tree painting. Green was her favourite colour of all.

She put yellow paint on her brush. Then she put blue on the same brush. She brushed it on the paper. But the green came out muddy and brown. "Oh no," said Zoe. "My leaf looks like mud."

Her friend Mia looked over. "Rinse your brush," Mia said. Zoe dipped her brush in the water cup. She swished it around. The water turned grey. She wiped the brush on a paper towel.

Now Zoe put yellow on the clean brush. Then she put blue. She brushed the paper. Bright green! Like a magic dragon, green and shiny. Zoe laughed and painted a big green leaf, then another, then ten more.

"Look," said Zoe politely to her teacher. "My tree has leaves." The teacher smiled. Zoe held up her brush. "Next, red and yellow," she said. "I will make dragon fire."

Olivier sat in the doctor's waiting room. He was not late. Mommy had brought him on time. He looked at a picture of a plane on the wall with his eyes. He heard music playing with his ears.

Then the doctor's office door opened. Behind it, a big machine started to hum. It got very loud. Olivier did not like the loud sound. He covered his ears with his hands. The loud sound got quieter. He took his hands away. It was loud again. He put his hands back. Quiet again.

"Loud, quiet, loud, quiet," said Olivier.

"You found a trick," said Mommy with a smile.

Soon the big machine stopped. The waiting room was calm. The nurse called them in. "Open your mouth," said the doctor. Olivier stuck out his tongue. He touched a sticker with his finger. It felt bumpy. It smelled like strawberries.

The doctor gave him a paper to draw on. Olivier drew a plane and two big hands over two little ears.

Ivy went to the cemetery with Dad and Gran. They visited Gran Gran's stone. Gran laid down dry flowers. Then Gran unpacked a picnic on the grass.

"First we say our blessing," said Gran. Ivy folded her hands. Gran said, "Thank you for this food." Then they ate.

Ivy bit her apple. "Who grew my apple?" she asked. "A farmer far away," said Dad. Ivy thought hard. Somebody picked the apple. Somebody baked the bread. Somebody carried them all the way here.

Ivy wanted to say thank you too. But her mouth was full. She chewed and chewed. She swallowed. Too late! The blessing was done. Ivy felt a lump in her throat, like a stone.

"Can we say it again?" she asked. "Blessings can wait for you," said Gran. Ivy took a big breath. "Thank you for the apple. One, two, three, thank yous," she said. "For the farmer, the baker, and Gran Gran." Dad smiled wide. Gran wiped her eye with her sleeve. The wind moved the grass, soft and slow.

Then Ivy reached for the bread and took the biggest piece she could choose. "Gran Gran liked bread too," she said.

Milan was at the park with his dad. He saw a red berry basket on the picnic mat. "Can I taste one?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "They are sweet strawberries."

Milan picked one up. His eyes saw the bright red. His hands felt the bumpy little seeds. His nose smelled something sweet. His ears heard a bird singing in the tree.

Milan pinched his nose closed. Then he took a bite. He blinked. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. He let go of his nose. Sniff! Now the sweet taste came back, strong again.

"Wow," he said. "My nose was closed and the taste went away!" He tried it again, just to know for sure. The taste got small again.

"How lucky I have a nose," said Milan. He took a big sniff of the basket. "My nose works like an elephant's big nose, right Dad?"

Dad laughed. "An elephant's nose can do even more. It can spray water!"

Milan held the last strawberry. He smelled it first. Then he ate it up.

Abigail woke up and looked out the window. The world was white. "Snow!" she said. "No school today." Mom said, "We can go to the park." Abigail ran to get dressed. She put on her warm coat. She put on her boots. She put on her hat. She ran out the door.

At the park, Abigail made a big snowball. She clapped her mittens together. Then she stopped. "Where are my mittens?" Her hands were bare. Her fingers turned cold, then colder. They hurt. "Ow," said Abigail. "My fingers are too cold." Mom said, "Let's go back for your mittens." They walked home fast.

Abigail put on her mittens. Her fingers got warm again. Back at the park, she made snowballs with happy hands. Then she saw something in the snow. A small green frog sat there, with wide eyes. "Hello, frog," said Abigail. The frog hopped away, and Abigail waved. "Bye, frog!" she called.

Lily was at school. It was nap time. The room was dark. "Is it night?" Lily whispered. She looked out the window. The sky was black. "It is dark like night," she said.

But then the teacher turned on a small light. The light was warm. Outside, the snow was cold on the glass. Lily touched the window with one finger. "Cold," she said. The light was not cold. The light was hot, so Teacher held it up high, away from little hands.

Lily wanted to know if it was night or morning. She got up slowly. She walked past the big blocks and the small blocks. One, two, three, four friends were sleeping. A snail sat in a jar. Its shell was big. Its body was slimy. "Hello, snail," said Lily.

The teacher smiled. "Look out now," she said. Lily looked. The sky was not black anymore. It was getting light. "Night goes away, and day comes," said the teacher. "Night and day are opposites." Lily watched the light grow. A bird flew by, fast. A cloud moved, slow. "It's morning!" Lily shouted. The snail slid up its jar. Lily clapped her hands. "One, two, three," she counted. "Three friends wake up!"

Ivy had to wait for the doctor. She held her teddy on her lap. Then teddy fell down. He slipped under the big coat on the chair. The room was dark there. Ivy looked and looked. She could not see teddy.

"Let's be a team," said Nurse Ann. First Ivy used her eyes to look. Her ears heard the paper crinkle. Her nose smelled soap. She touched the soft coat with her hands. Still no teddy. "It is hard to see in the dark," said Nurse Ann. She reached up and turned on the light. The bright light made the dark corner bright. There was teddy!

"Now I can see him with my eyes," said Ivy. She hugged teddy tight. He was not grumpy at all. The doctor came in. He looked in Ivy's ears. He looked in her mouth. "Say ahh," he said. Ivy laughed. "Ahh," she said.

Luke put on his red shoes. Today he would get his very own library card! He ran into the storytime room. It had round rugs and big soft mats. Miss Kim smiled at him.

"Here is your card, Luke," she said. Luke held it with two hands. It was his! Now he could take a book home.

Luke found a book about a tiny seed that grows into a big sunflower. He loved it. But he put it back on the wrong shelf. Miss Kim turned the book. "See the label on the spine," she said. "It shows where the book belongs." The label had letters on it. Luke looked at the other books. They had labels too! He pushed his book next to the matching ones. It fit just right.

"Good job, Luke," said Miss Kim. Luke checked out his book. He hugged it all the way home. "Let's read it now!" he said.

Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He wanted a stuffed animal. "Pick one!" said Mama.

First they walked past the toys. Balls and trucks sat on a long shelf. Then they saw the animal shelf. A dog! A cow! Isaiah hugged a soft dog. "This is an animal," he said. Mama smiled.

Next they passed the fish tank. A little fish swam round and round. "Fish is not an animal," said Isaiah. "It has no legs!" A big boy leaned close to the glass. "Fish are animals too," he said. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Isaiah's eyes got big. "Wow! The fish is an animal!"

Isaiah ran back to the shelf. He could not forget that fish. He picked the dog in one hand. Then he pointed at a fish toy. "Mama! Can I have an animal that swims?"

Mama laughed. "You can have both." She put the dog and the fish in the cart. Isaiah waved at the fish tank. "Bye, animal!" Then they went to get juice, and Isaiah held his fish all the way home.

Evelyn woke up. She heard the kettle. She saw Mom and Dad at the table. "Good morning," Evelyn said. Mom smiled wide. "It is morning now. That means we wake up and eat breakfast." Evelyn ate her egg. Then she said, "Now can we go to the park?"

"Today we can," said Mom. "Yesterday the park was wet from rain. Today it is dry." Evelyn put on her shoes. She took her present for Nia, a small red ball. She had gotten it yesterday.

At the park, Nia was already on the swing. "Good morning," Evelyn said. Nia laughed. "It is not morning now. We ate breakfast before, and now it is play time." Evelyn held out the red ball. "A present for you." Nia took it and hugged it.

They rolled the ball back and forth. Once it stopped in the grass. They waited. A wind came, and the grass moved, but the ball stayed. Evelyn ran and got it. They rolled it again and again. "Tomorrow we come back," said Nia. "Yes," said Evelyn. "Tomorrow." She threw the ball one more time, high and wide, and Nia caught it.

Elena woke up at Grandma's house. The kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma was baking cookies. Elena wanted one so much.

"May I have a cookie, please?" Elena asked. Grandma smiled and gave her a warm cookie. "Thank you," Elena said. The cookie was soft and yummy.

Then Grandma said, "Put on your shoes. We will go to the park before it gets late." The air was cool and fresh outside. At the park, a boy was digging in the sand. His shovel fell. Elena picked it up for him.

"Gracias," the boy said. Elena blinked. She did not know that word. "It means thank you," Grandma said softly. "Other languages have their own words for it." So thank you was not the same everywhere.

Elena tried the new word. "Gracias!" she said. The boy laughed and dug a big hole. Then he poured water in. "Look, it can swim," he said, floating his little boat on top. Elena clapped her hands.

On the walk home, Elena stepped on Grandma's toe by mistake. "Sorry," she said. "That's all right," said Grandma. At the door, Elena asked, "Can you help me with my coat, please?" Grandma helped her.

Then Grandma gave her one more cookie, right before dinner, just because. Elena held it in both hands. "Gracias," she said. Grandma hugged her tight.

Madeline woke up on festival day. The house smelled like sweet cookies. Mama was lighting little lamps on the table. "Today we celebrate," Mama said.

Madeline looked at her play clothes. "I want to wear my shorts," she said. Then she saw Papa come out in his best blue shirt. Grandma came out in her gold shawl. Even Baby Sam had a tiny red hat on.

Madeline ran to her room. She found her purple dress with stars. She put it on all by herself. She looked in the mirror and smiled.

At dinner, Grandma gave her a sweet. "It will make your tooth happy," Grandma said with a laugh. Outside, rain began to fall, but the lamps still glowed. Madeline twirled in her dress. "Now I look like festival day," she said.

Matteo put on his swim shorts. He ran to the pool door. "Wait!" Dad called. "We take a shower first."

Matteo stopped. "A shower?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in." Matteo looked at the little shower by the wall. The water was warm. It made his hair thick and wet.

Then Matteo saw a girl run past. She jumped up and down. "I want the pool!" she shouted. A lifeguard held up one hand. "Shower first," the lifeguard said. The girl looked at the shower. The water went splish, splish. She ran under it and laughed.

"Your turn," said Dad. Matteo stood under the warm water. It ran down his nose. "Now the pool?" he asked. "Now the pool," said Dad. Matteo walked to the steps. He kicked his legs in the blue water. "I did it!" he shouted. "I showered, and then I swam!" Dad clapped his hands. "Look at you, Matteo!" said Dad. "Look at you go!"

Arthur sat on the big couch. He had a sock on each foot and a warm blanket on his lap. His nose was red and his throat felt scratchy. He coughed one small cough.

"I want to run outside," said Arthur. He slid his feet to the floor. "Not yet," said Mama. "You have a cold. First we rest here. Then your body can get better." Arthur frowned. His face felt sour and grumpy.

Mama brought his favourite book. Arthur looked at the pictures. He found a cat, a moon, and a red boat. "Where is the frog?" he asked. He turned the page. There it was! Arthur let out a happy sound. He drank a little water from his cup.

He rested his head on the pillow. His eyes got heavy. He slept for a long time. When he woke up, he sniffed the air. Soup! His nose could smell again. He sat up tall. "My body feels better," said Arthur. He hugged the soft blanket tight. "Can we read the frog book one more time?"

James ran into writing club. "I want to write my name today!" he said. Ms. Rosa smiled. She gave him a fat pencil and showed him how to hold it. "Pinch it like this," she said. "Now pick your letters."

James looked at his name card. J, A, M, E, S. Ms. Rosa had put the letters in two trays. One tray was full of straight letters. A went in. M went in. E went in. The other tray had curvy letters. J went there. S went there too.

"That one pops right in the curvy tray," said James. He laughed.

Then he wrote. Straight lines for A. Curves for S. His letters made a word. "JAMES! I did it!" he shouted. "My name popped onto the paper!"

Evan ran to the block corner. He wanted the big red blocks. He was the last one there. Mia had them first.

"My turn!" Evan shouted. His voice was very loud.

Then he heard a small sound. It went "wah, wah." The teacher's baby was sleeping in a little bed by the window. The teacher put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she whispered. "The baby is sleeping. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice."

Evan made his voice tiny. "My turn?" he whispered. Mia nodded. "You can have some blocks. I will share." Evan dug into the bin. He found a long stick block. He held it up. "Look what I found," he whispered. Mia smiled and took a quiet turn with it too.

The baby kept sleeping. The room was soft and calm. Evan whispered, "Is the baby still asleep?" Mia peeked with him. "Yes," she said. "We were quiet."

The baby woke up and blinked. The teacher said, "Time for snack now." Evan whispered, "The baby can come too."

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of many shapes. She found a circle block. It rolled away. She found a triangle block. It had three pointy sides.

Then she found a square block. It had four sides, all the same. Perfect for the snake house door! She set it down flat. "A door!" she said.

Her brother Ben ran in. He turned the square block. Now a corner pointed up. "Look, a new shape!" said Ben.

Lillian frowned. That was not the door she made. She turned the block back. The corner went down. The flat side sat on the floor again. It was the same square! Four sides, all the same.

"Same square!" said Lillian.

"You are right," said Ben. "That is so silly of me!"

Lillian laughed. She stacked two more squares. She made a roof with the triangle. The snake had a house at last. Lillian clapped her hands and hugged the snake.

Sienna sat in her car seat. She hugged her brown teddy. But Bunny was gone. "Bunny is lost," she said. Her tummy felt worried.

Mama turned around from the front seat. "Don't worry. We will find Bunny," she said. "First we go home. Then we retrace our steps."

"What is that?" asked Sienna.

"It means going back to each place we went, in order," said Mama.

The car stopped at home. Sienna ran to the porch. She looked by the door. No Bunny. Next, they drove to the shop. Sienna looked at the bread shelf. No Bunny. Last, they drove to the park.
