Sienna walked back along the path. First she stopped at the swings. She looked under the seat. No Bunny. Then she stopped at the slide. There, at the bottom, was Bunny! Sienna picked her up.

"Retracing worked!" said Sienna. She hugged Bunny tight. "Thank you, Mama," she said.

Back in the car, the warm sun came in. The lamp post glowed outside. Bunny sat beside teddy on the seat. Sienna closed her eyes. "Home soon," she whispered. Mama smiled and drove on.

Ellie went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find her favorite book. It was a book about a bunny. But the bunny book was not on the shelf.

Ellie looked by the fish tank. No bunny book. She looked by the big pillows. No bunny book. Then she heard music. It came from the playroom.

A boy named Sam was cleaning up. "Blocks, dolls and balls," he said. He put each toy in the toy box. "Blocks, dolls and balls. Blocks, dolls and balls." Ellie watched him. She picked up a ball. She put it in the box too. Sam smiled. Then Ellie saw something under the chair. It was a red book. It had a bunny on the cover!

"You found it," said Sam. Ellie hugged the book. She sat on a big pillow. Her dad read to her. Ellie got sleepy. She closed her eyes, just for a little bit. "Blocks, dolls and balls," she whispered. "And one bunny book."

Beatrice went to the store with Mama and baby Sam. She put apples in the cart. Sam took the apples out. Beatrice put them in again. Sam pulled them out again. "Sam, you are being silly," said Beatrice. Did Sam want the cart empty?

Mama smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. Beatrice put a big melon in the cart. It was too big for Sam's hands. It stayed in! Beatrice put a small plum in too. Sam took the small plum out. Out it came, fast. Beatrice laughed.

Then they passed the bakery. The bread was hot. Mama picked it up with a cloth, slow and careful. "Hot bread can hurt," said Mama. Beatrice touched the cold milk carton instead. It felt nice.

At the checkout, Beatrice had her answer. Sam just liked taking things out. So she gave him a soft bun to hold. Sam held it. Nothing went in. Nothing came out. The cart rolled away, full.

Max wanted the red truck. Ben had the red truck. Max grabbed for it. Miss Ana put her hand out. "We wait," she said. Max sat on the pillow. The pillow was itchy. He wiggled and waited.

Then Ben held out the truck. "Your turn," said Ben. Max took it. He remembered something. "Thank you, Ben," he said. Ben smiled big. Ben gave him a hug.

Max pushed the truck across the rug. It went far. It went under the doll house. A tiny mouse toy was hiding there! "Look!" said Max. Ben laughed. "You found him," said Ben. "My turn now," said Max, holding out the truck.

Eva wants to find the cat book at the library. She grabs a big red book from the shelf. She sits down and opens it.

But the pictures look funny. The cat is upside down! His tail hangs by his ears. His whiskers point at the floor.

"Hello, silly cat," says Eva. "You are upside down!"

The librarian smiles. "Books go this way," she says, turning the book around.

Now the cat stands on his feet. Eva looks at the squiggly marks under the cat. "That says cat," says the librarian. Eva points at each mark. The words tell the cat where to sit.

Eva turns one page, then the next page. The cat walks through the snow on the last page. "The end," says Eva, and she pats the book.

Amira was going to a new place. Mama held her hand in the big hall. "We look for door five," said Mama. Amira wanted to find it first.

They walked past door 1. Then door 2. Then door 3. Amira counted on her fingers. "One, two, three," she said. Her sock began to scratch her heel, so she stopped to wiggle her foot.

Then Amira saw a sign. It said 5. She held up her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "Mama, look! It is five!"

"Yes," said Mama with a smile. "That means five." She knocked on door 5.

Grandpa opened the door. "You found me!" he said. He gave Amira a big hug. "Come and see my world of buttons," he said. He had jars of buttons, all colors.

Amira counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten buttons in the red jar. Grandpa clapped.

It was snack time at school. Ruby had a job. She had to put out the cups. There were ten chairs at the table. Ruby held a stack of shiny cups.

She put one cup in front of one chair. "One cup, one chair," she said. She put a cup at the next chair too. "One cup, one chair." She went all the way around the table. Each chair got one cup.

At the last chair, her hand was empty. Ruby looked in the stack. No cups were left. She asked herself, "Do we have the same number of cups and chairs?" She counted the cups. Ten cups. She counted the chairs. Ten chairs. Each cup had one chair. Each chair had one cup. So yes, the same number.

Then Ben came with a string of crackers on a red thread. He had eight crackers. Ruby counted them. Ben asked, "Who has more, me or the table?" Ruby looked. The table had ten cups. Ben had eight crackers. "The table has more," she said. Ben lifted his string and laughed. Then everyone sat down, one cup in front of each chair, and the snack began.

Luke went to the mall with his mom. He was going to get his very first haircut. The salon had a big fish tank. The fish were blue and orange. They swam low in the water, then up, then low again.

Luke sat in the big chair. The hairdresser, Meg, put a low board across his lap. Then she picked up her scissors. But Luke heard a pop-pop sound. He turned to look at the fish tank. Snip went the scissors in the wrong place. "Oops," said Meg. "Your head moved."

Luke wondered, "If I sit still, will my hair look nice?" He tried it. He sat like a statue. He looked straight at the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little feathers on his arm. It tickled. Meg smiled. "Look now," she said. Luke saw a neat, short haircut in the mirror. "You sat very still," said Meg. "That helped me cut it neatly."

Mom brought Luke's jacket. On the way out, Luke stopped by the fish tank. One fish came up to the glass. It looked at him and did not move at all. Luke laughed. "You sit still too," he said. "Goodbye, fish."

Leah saw a big cardboard box at school. She wanted to play with it. "A house!" said Leah. She put her doll inside and gave the doll a pretend bottle.

Then Ben came. "A car!" said Ben. He wanted the box too. "It is my house," said Leah. "It is my car," said Ben. Their teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "You can take turns," she said. "First the house. Then the car."

Leah fed her doll. She tucked her in with a small cloth. Then she said, "Your turn, Ben." Ben sat in the box. "Beep beep!" he said. He drove the car fast. Leah held his pretend bucket of gas and filled the tank.

After that, Ben tipped the box onto its side. "Now it is a boat!" he said. Leah climbed in too. They rowed across the pretend sea. The doll sat between them and looked out. "Faster!" said Leah. The boat rocked hard, so they rowed slow. Then Miss Kim called, "Snack time!" They hurried out of the boat and left it floating on the blue rug.

Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad held her hand. They walked to the playground.

A boy was hiding behind his mom. He peeked out at Violet. He did not say a word. Violet wanted a friend to play with. She waved and said, "Hello!" The boy peeked out more. "Hello," he said back. His mom smiled. "Let's go on the swings," said the boy.

Violet ran to the swings. She sat down. But the swing would not go. Her coat felt itchy and stuck. "Dad, can you help, please?" she asked. Dad gave the swing a little push. Up went Violet, high like a bird. The boy swung next to her. "Thank you," said Violet to Dad. Dad laughed and pushed them both again and again.

Asher went to the store with Mama. He wanted a book about trucks. He found one with a big red truck on the front. He hugged it. It was soft and smooth.

Asher opened the book. But wait. The pages looked all mixed up. He turned one page. Then another page. Then another. "Silly book," said Asher. "Your truck is hiding!"

Mama smiled. "Turn the book around," she said. Asher flipped it over. Now the truck was on the front. He opened the front cover. Page one, page two, page three. The story made sense now. The truck went beep, beep!

"Read it to me all day," said Asher. "Front to back, front to back." Mama laughed. "Front to back it is." They sat down on a little red seat. Asher turned the pages, one by one, all the way to the back cover. Then he turned the book over and started again.

Sarah sat at a big desk in the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. A game was on. Her family and friends watched too.

The red team ran fast. The blue team ran fast too. Sarah clapped her hands and shouted, "Go red team!" But everyone at the table went quiet. Then Daddy said, "We like the blue team, sweetie." Sarah giggled. "Oops. I am sorry, blue team!"

Then the blue team kicked the ball in the net. Everyone jumped up. They cheered and clapped for the blue team. Sarah clapped too. She clapped so hard her hands felt warm.

"Now I know," Sarah said. "You clap when your team scores!" She smiled and waved her little flag. The waiter brought lemonade for everyone. Sarah took a big sip. "Go blue team!" she shouted, one more time.

Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big basket of apples. She wanted the bright red apple on top.

Avery reached out and grabbed for it. Another little boy was reaching too. The basket wobbled. Mama held it steady. "One at a time," said the store man. The boy went first. He took one apple and said, "Thank you."

Then it was Avery's turn. She took the bright red apple. She held it with both hands. Mama said, "We say please when we ask for something." Avery looked at the store man. "Please," she said. He smiled and gave her a little sticker.

At the checkout, they waited in the line. Avery stood by the cart. A man let them go ahead. "You can go first," he said. "Thank you," said Mama. Avery waved her sticker. At home, she sat on her pillow and held her apple. "Please," she said to Mama, "can I have a bite?" "Yes, you can," said Mama, and she cut the apple into slices.

Kayden woke up in the dark. "Is it morning now?" he asked. He heard a plane go by, high in the sky. It was still night. Night was not morning yet.

He felt shy in the dark hallway. He went to find Dad. Dad said, "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast. It is not morning yet. It is morning later, when the sun comes up." Kayden climbed into the big bed. Dad tucked the blanket around him.

"Now we sleep," said Dad. "Tomorrow is morning. Yesterday was morning too, and you ate eggs." Kayden thought about eggs. Yesterday he had eggs. Today he would have pancakes. He wanted pancakes so much.

The sun came up. It was morning now! Kayden ran to the kitchen. Mom was at the table. "Good morning, Kayden," she said. She had made pancakes. Kayden ate three. He did not cry about the dark night anymore. Morning was here at last, just like Dad said.

He licked the syrup off his fork. "Today is a good day," he said.

Ibrahim was at the park with his little red car. He put it down on the grass. Then he ran to the swings. When he came back, the car was gone.

"I lost my car," he said. Mama came to help. They looked by the slide. They looked by the tree. No car. "Let me try one more spot," said Mama. "Small toys can roll under couches and beds." She pointed down low. Ibrahim got on his knees. He looked under the long park bench.

There it was. The red car had rolled under the bench. Its little wheels were still spinning. The ground under the bench was cool and shady. A small black bug walked past the car, slow and calm. "Hello, bug," said Ibrahim. He reached in with his whole arm. His fingers touched the smooth red roof. He pulled the car out and held it up to the sun. It was warm on top from sitting in the light.

Mama laughed. "That was the last place I thought to look," she said. Ibrahim put the car in his pocket, safe and snug. They walked home talking about winter, and how the leaves would fall soon. In his pocket, the car went bump, bump, bump with every step.

Hunter ran into the big hall. There were balloons on the wall. There was a table with a cake. Grandma held the cake carefully. Four little candles stood on top. Daddy lit the candles with a match. Hunter watched from his chair.

A girl named Mia came over. She had a feather in her hair. "You can touch it," she said. Hunter touched the feather. It was soft. Then Mia asked, "How old are you?"

Hunter held up three fingers. "I am three," he said. Mia shook her head. "No. Today is your birthday," she said. "On your birthday, you turn one year older."

Hunter looked at his fingers. He put one more finger up. One, two, three, four. "I am four now!" he said. Grandma smiled. She held the cake near him. "Be careful," she said. "The candles are little flames." Hunter blew and blew. The flames went out. Everyone clapped.

Then everyone sang. Hunter sat up tall. Four candles, four years old. "I will be five next time," he said. Daddy laughed and gave him a big hug.

Charles went to the art studio with his mama. He brought his box of crayons. The box had been in the car all morning. The sun had shone on the car all day.

Charles opened the box. He picked up his red crayon. It bent like a worm! He picked up his blue crayon. It bent too. "My crayons are soft," said Charles. "They are all bendy!"

His crayons would not draw. The red one just made a shiny smear. Charles tried again. He pressed very gently. Still no line, just a smear. "I want to draw a dog," said Charles.

The art teacher came over. Her name was Mia. "Let's try something," she said. She held the bendy crayons near the warm art studio oven. The crayons got softer and softer. Charles watched from his stool. Mia dripped the melted red onto thick paper. It made a shiny red dot!

Then Charles had an idea. He held up a stick from the craft table. "Can we mix the colors on my stick?" he asked. Mia dripped red, then blue, then yellow onto the stick. The colors ran down together. They made a shiny rainbow stick!

Charles waited and waited while it dried. He held it up to the window. "My bendy crayons made a magic stick," said Charles. "Can we leave the box in the sunny car again tomorrow?"

Yesterday Athena went to the store with Mom. Today they went again. Athena wanted the pink yogurt with the strawberry on it. Yesterday the shelf was empty. Today she hoped it was there.

Athena ran to the dairy case. She looked and looked. The pink yogurt was not there. A man in a green shirt was stacking milk. "Excuse me," said Athena. "Do you have the pink yogurt?"

"The truck comes today," said the man. "More yogurt soon."

"Soon?" asked Athena.

"Soon means in a little while," said the man. "Not a long wait."

Athena tapped her toes. She counted to ten. Then the doors opened wide. A big truck backed up slow. Men rolled in boxes on a noisy cart. Athena watched from her spot by the cart.

"Now we can stock the shelf," said the man. He opened a box. He put out pink yogurt, row after row.

"There it is!" said Athena. She took two. Mom smiled and put them in the cart.

"Later we will eat one," said Mom. "Tomorrow we can have the other one. Can you show me where the bus stop is?"

Athena pointed out the window. "The bus will come soon," she said.

The bus rolled up. Athena held Mom's hand. In her bag, the pink yogurt sat cold and safe. The doors opened with a hiss. "All aboard," called the driver.
